en: Known as a weighty, formidable hero,
Tending his millet until hard as stone,
Praising his wife as though she were a maiden,
With yurt-lattices of wood,
His forefathers of Alash—
Hero Kokcho, son of Aidarkan,
Was a son-in-law too.
They bound up their pinewood spears;
On account of Aktulpar,
That son-in-law left and turned to war.
The two khans, Ezhigei and Zhanchy,
Were sons-in-law too.
They became malicious, quarrelsome adversaries;
On account of Aktulpar,
Those two khans became enemies.
Young Manas, son of Khan Zhakyp,
To your grandfather, this Khan Temir,
Was a son-in-law too.
Then, with golden forelock and tasseled belt,
The only son of Khan Azyz in Beezhin,
The tips of his ears already pierced,
When he was born into the world,
Already circumcised,
His forehead touched the earth.
When my dear Ala came into the world,
Crying from the womb, reciting the creed,
In Beezhin of Kakan-Chyn,
Rain fell for eighty days,
And an earthquake struck.
His waist bent soft as cotton.
The renowned name of my Almam
Was inscribed in the register
Of Kary Khan, khan of Beezhin.
He saw a saint in a dream;
He beheld heaven and hell.
He saw souls in grievous torment.
Leaving the dark faith, he became pure;
Fleeing the unbelievers, he became estranged.
He scattered all he had amassed,
Set his sights on faith alone,
Stained the golden throne with blood.
Saying, “He will not enter the Muslim faith,
He will not go toward Islam with me,”
He killed his father, Khan Azyz,
In broad Beezhin.
Staining the silver throne with blood,
He killed his father, Kun Zhang-Zhung.
Escaping where death had seemed certain,
With Konurbai, son of Alooke,
He fought fiercely for six months.
When he scattered his treasure and possessions,
When he fled toward Islam,
We heard rumors and reports:
The lion Almam, wolf-like hero,
We heard, had entered Altai,
Overthrown the khan of Altai,
And, unable to find his place there,
Had entered Khangai, we heard.
The people of Khangai, those folk,
The Black Kalmyks and the Manchus,
He had slaughtered, we heard.
Finding no place in Khangai,
Traversing every region,
Among the human creatures on the earth,
Leaving not one unvisited,
Exulting in his valor,
My dear Ala met many people.
We heard he came to Kokcho;
We heard he besieged
Kokcho of the Kazakhs.
Because of his friend's wife Akerkech,
We heard he battered the Kazakh,
Beating him with resounding blows.
With hero Mazhik following him,
Paying heed to no one,
Almam departed alone, we heard.
Leaving Sary-Arka,
Your valiant, wolf-like Almam
Reached that very Mecca,
We heard.
When he was returning from Mecca,
When my brave Alma was returning,
When God was to grant his wish,
When the lion Almam was coming,
The multitude of Kyrgyz moved toward the lowlands
And were encamped there.
Kymyz by day, maidens by night—
While they were living so,
Your father Manas, the leopard,
Awoke with a start from sleep,
Turned onto his right side,
Dipped his hands in water,
Performed the washing of his hands,
And had five nines of animals, headed by a mare,
Slaughtered as moon-hoofed sacrifices.
Hero Bakai of saintly wisdom
And Khan Koshoi of the Katagan
He summoned to interpret his dream.
“Koshoi, Bakai, my saints,
My elders arisen from the Kyrgyz!
Your blessing never goes astray,
Fathers of many peoples,
Your blessings enrich the people,
My elders with the nature of prophets.
That precious land of Zheti-Suu,
You made it a homeland by your skill.
The Kyrgyz of Zheti-Suu
You brought together into a people.
Hero Bakai of saintly wisdom,
You found sight in the dark night,
Found the right words in a sudden crisis.
Going before me, you bring good fortune;
Sent into battle, you are like countless troops.
The great ones of these Kyrgyz,
The falcons of the world's peoples,
The two khans, Koshoi and Bakai:
As I slept, I had a dream.
I saw a mighty thing in my dream.
I saw a ridge full of treasure,
I saw a ravenous lion,
I saw a blaze of red-hot coals,
Such as exists nowhere in the world.
Born in the east,
Its appearance washed pure white,
Growing wild when its hood was removed,
King of the animal creatures,
Roused when it saw a lion,
Not drawing back from a bear,
Not retreating at the sight of a tiger—
An eagle came to me in my dream.
Nothing it struck was left alive;
Nothing it swooped upon returned alive.
Sixty lions
I had it catch by setting it upon them.
When I set it upon a boar, it did not strike.
Of the eagle upon my arm,
Nothing it flew at remained alive.
This dream I have told you,
Elders Bakai and Koshoi,
Interpret it, and I shall have no regret.”
Bakai and Koshoi said this:
“When one champion meets another,
It is a remedy granted by the Lord.
The only son of Kakan Khan in Beezhin—
It is the coming of Almam the leopard.
Your ravenous lion, your falcon,
The eagle you carry—
It is the only son of Khan Azozyl.
That dear man named Almambet
Will bring plenty to your household.
If Almambet comes,
He will make you a majestic khan.
Sixty lions
Your eagle caught for you:
To Beezhin, beyond the Four Companions' reach,
It means your strength will reach.
Almambet will meet you,
Of Beezhin, that place of towering strength,
He will scout the approaches.
Against Beezhin, which Iskender never touched,
He will perform your service.
If Almambet comes into your hands,
My son, you will drive white deer and make them cattle,
Throw the whole world into confusion.
You will drive gray deer and make them cattle,
Throw every land you see into confusion.
That fierce white-shouldered eagle with its neck-guard,
That will not retreat before a lion,
Is Almambet himself.
Settling with his household in Talas,
Becoming your friend,
Hero, he is about to join you!”
“I have another dream, another still;
Khans, interpret this one too!
Last night I had a dream,
I saw a possession beyond compare.
When I raged, it came to me.
As I set out
On a journey to the east,
Right there in the open plain,
Without a sheath to put it in,
I found a naked sword.
When I struck iron as vast as Ala-Too,
It never rebounded without cutting through.
What twelve ages had never wrought,
In all this world,
No one remained who could withstand me.
If that steel from my dream
Comes into my hands, I shall have no regret!
What could this mean,
The two khans, Koshoi and Bakai?
Uncles, interpret this dream for me!”
Then Bakai spoke thus
And interpreted the dream:
“Your falcon born of light,
Born among unbelievers and grown mighty,
Your dear ravenous lion—
When God made Almam,
When your dear Ala was born,
The tips of his ears were pierced;
He came crying from the womb, they say.
Already circumcised,
His forehead touched the earth, they say.
When I ask those versed in tradition,
In twelve-gated Beezhin,
For eighty days and nights,
Hail and rain fell without cease,
And earthquakes struck, they say.
The great ones of the Chinese,
All the sorcerers,
Those who had studied wonders—
All their diviners,
Asked, ‘Which is the child Almam?
Which is the child who has brought
Turmoil upon the whole world?
Which is the child who will overthrow
And slaughter all the khans?’
As turmoil fell upon Beezhin
And they could not find the child,
His mother Altynai
Had an amulet hung about his neck,
Held him close against her breast.
‘They will torment my child,’ she said.
Misleading them about her child,
She had her father Sooronduk rear him.
Letting no one suspect,
Letting not a single person know,
As the son of Khan Azyz,
She guarded, nurtured, and raised him.
They had Sarala saddled.
When he reached seven years,
They had him taught wondrous knowledge.
He grew to manhood as a hero,
Equal to the sons of heroes.
When he reached twelve,
Dust rose wherever he went.
‘If Almambet lives,
He will cause some marvel!’ they said,
And Ez-kara nearly died of fright.
When he reached twelve,
He slipped quietly away and lost himself.
In the hollow of Kyr-Kaiyng,
Along Khan-Zhailak,
Contending for the mountains of Chai-Kent—
From those who came, I heard news:
In the desert of Mediyan,
Konurbai, son of Alooke,
From atop Algara,
Six times that Kalcha
He knocked down into the ground, I heard.
Hero Almam alone, out of Beezhin,
Until the soft kurai stems ripened,
Until the autumn gossamer flew,
Kept fighting, I heard.
Escaping death,
He saw Beijing's people.
